Architecture proposal

Solver Outputs

A separate, extensible data plane for optional diagnostics produced by a solver—requested by consumers, allocated by the solver, populated during step(), and consumed by sensors, viewers, and applications.

  • solver-owned
  • set-composable flags
  • allocate once, reuse
  • custom-solver extensible
  • fail-fast validation
Core rule: simulation state stores the data needed to advance the simulation. Optional data that a solver can report—but the simulation does not need to continue—belongs in SolverOutputs.

Why change the ownership model?

Extended attributes made the model responsible for requesting data that only a solver can produce. This inverted ownership, expanded every state/contact allocation, and made it hard for a custom solver to expose new diagnostics.

Before — extended attributes

Consumer mutates model allocation policy

Sensor or application
↓ request_state_attribute(...)
Model / ModelBuilder
↓ allocates every State or Contacts
State.body_parent_f / Contacts.force
  • The model appears to own solver capabilities.
  • Optional diagnostics are mixed into persistent simulation data.
  • Custom solver outputs need global model/state plumbing.
  • Allocation intent is implicit and can happen far from the solver.
After — solver outputs

Consumers declare needs; solver owns allocation

Sensors / viewer / application
↓ union solver_output_flags
solver.outputs(flags)
↓ validates + allocates concrete type
SolverOutputs
  • The request is made against the component that produces the data.
  • Only requested arrays are allocated.
  • Standard and solver-specific flags compose in one set.
  • The same container flows explicitly to every consumer.

Proposed architecture

The design separates the persistent simulation data plane from an optional diagnostic data plane. Allocation occurs once during setup; production and consumption occur every step without changing the model.

Class and extension model

Design contracts

A small number of strict contracts keep extension safe and make configuration errors fail during setup instead of silently corrupting data at runtime.

Flags are plain Enum members

Standard and custom enum members coexist in a set without coordinating bit ranges. IntEnum, raw strings, and string-mixin enums are rejected because value equality can collide across independent extensions.

Unsupported requests fail at allocation

Every solver advertises supported_output_flags. A request outside that set raises immediately, before a simulation loop or graph capture begins.

Containers belong to one solver instance

The allocator records solver ownership. Passing the container to another solver is rejected, preventing compatible-looking arrays from being filled with the wrong semantics.

Contact outputs bind to contact storage

CONTACT_F requires the exact Contacts instance used for sizing and stepping, preserving capacity and index alignment for sensors and viewers.

Unrequested fields stay None

The concrete type is stable, but buffers are opt-in. Consumers can inspect flags or fields without allocating every diagnostic supported by the solver.

Allocation is reusable and graph-friendly

Allocate before stepping and reuse the same arrays. There is no per-step Python allocation, which keeps the design compatible with CUDA graph capture.

Standard flagOutput fieldMeaningShape / binding
BODY_QDDbody_qddRigid-body spatial acceleration(body_count,)
BODY_PARENT_Fbody_parent_fIncoming parent-joint wrench at child COM(body_count,)
CONTACT_Fcontact_fSpatial contact force aligned with contact indicesrigid_contact_max + soft_contact_max; bound to Contacts

How applications use it

The application gathers requirements from all consumers, allocates one container, and threads it explicitly through the solver step and downstream processing.

  1. Collect flagsUnion application needs with every sensor's solver_output_flags.
  2. Allocate onceCall solver.outputs(flags); pass contacts= when needed.
  3. Populate on stepPass the same container to solver.step(..., outputs=outputs).
  4. Consume resultsRead arrays directly or pass the container to sensors and viewers.

Body-level outputs

Allocate once during setup
from newton.solvers import SolverMuJoCo, SolverOutputFlags

solver = SolverMuJoCo(model)
outputs = solver.outputs(
    {
        SolverOutputFlags.BODY_QDD,
        SolverOutputFlags.BODY_PARENT_F,
    }
)

for _ in range(num_steps):
    solver.step(state_in, state_out, control, contacts, dt, outputs=outputs)

    acceleration = outputs.body_qdd
    parent_wrench = outputs.body_parent_f
    state_in, state_out = state_out, state_in

Contact-indexed outputs

Bind allocation to the contact container
pipeline = newton.CollisionPipeline(model)
contacts = pipeline.contacts()

outputs = solver.outputs(
    {SolverOutputFlags.CONTACT_F},
    contacts=contacts,
)

pipeline.collide(state_in, contacts)
solver.step(state_in, state_out, control, contacts, dt, outputs=outputs)

# Same ordering and capacity as `contacts`.
contact_force = outputs.contact_f

Extend it for a custom solver

A custom solver defines its own plain enum, derives a container that retains every standard field, advertises the combined supported set, and extends allocation and population for custom fields.

1. Define the custom flag and container

No global registry or bit allocation
from enum import Enum
import warp as wp

from newton.solvers import SolverOutputs


class ThermalOutputFlags(Enum):
    BODY_TEMPERATURE = "body_temperature"


class ThermalSolverOutputs(SolverOutputs):
    def __init__(self, flags=()):
        super().__init__(flags)
        self.body_temperature: wp.array[wp.float32] | None = None

2. Select the type and allocate custom fields

Call super() for standard arrays
from newton.solvers import SolverBase, SolverOutputFlags


class ThermalSolver(SolverBase):
    OUTPUTS_TYPE = ThermalSolverOutputs
    SUPPORTED_OUTPUT_FLAGS = frozenset(
        {
            SolverOutputFlags.BODY_QDD,
            ThermalOutputFlags.BODY_TEMPERATURE,
        }
    )

    def _allocate_outputs(self, outputs, *, requires_grad):
        super()._allocate_outputs(outputs, requires_grad=requires_grad)

        if ThermalOutputFlags.BODY_TEMPERATURE in outputs:
            outputs.body_temperature = wp.zeros(
                self.model.body_count,
                dtype=wp.float32,
                device=self.model.device,
                requires_grad=requires_grad,
            )

3. Validate and populate during the step

Only fill arrays that were requested
    def step(
        self,
        state_in,
        state_out,
        control,
        contacts,
        dt,
        *,
        outputs=None,
    ):
        self._validate_outputs(outputs, contacts)

        # ...advance simulation and populate standard outputs...

        if outputs is not None and outputs.body_temperature is not None:
            wp.launch(
                compute_body_temperature,
                dim=self.model.body_count,
                inputs=[state_out.body_qd],
                outputs=[outputs.body_temperature],
                device=self.model.device,
            )

4. Compose standard and custom requests

The caller treats both enums uniformly
requested = {
    SolverOutputFlags.BODY_QDD,
    ThermalOutputFlags.BODY_TEMPERATURE,
}

outputs = solver.outputs(requested)
solver.step(state_in, state_out, control, contacts, dt, outputs=outputs)

temperature = outputs.body_temperature

How sensors consume outputs

Sensors declare requirements without mutating the model. The application remains the orchestrator: it unions all consumer requirements, verifies that the selected solver supports them, and shares one populated container.

Combined IMU and contact sensor loop

Requirements remain composable
imu = newton.sensors.SensorIMU(model, sites="imu_*")
contact_sensor = newton.sensors.SensorContact(
    model,
    sensing_shapes="foot_*",
)

pipeline = newton.CollisionPipeline(model)
contacts = pipeline.contacts()

flags = imu.solver_output_flags | contact_sensor.solver_output_flags
outputs = solver.outputs(flags, contacts=contacts)

for _ in range(num_steps):
    pipeline.collide(state_in, contacts)
    solver.step(state_in, state_out, control, contacts, dt, outputs=outputs)

    imu.update(state_out, outputs=outputs)
    contact_sensor.update(state_out, contacts, outputs=outputs)
    viewer.log_contacts(contacts, state_out, outputs=outputs)

    state_in, state_out = state_out, state_in

What changes for existing code?

Legacy extended-attribute paths remain available for a deprecation window, but new code requests the equivalent output from the solver and passes the container explicitly.

Deprecated pathReplacementReason
State.body_qddoutputs.body_qddAcceleration is solver-produced diagnostic data.
State.body_parent_foutputs.body_parent_fJoint reaction reporting varies by solver capability.
State.mujoco.qfrc_actuatorSolverMuJoCo.Outputs.qfrc_actuatorSolver-specific diagnostics stay on the solver-specific container.
Contacts.forceoutputs.contact_fContact geometry and computed force have separate ownership.
model.request_state_attributes(...)solver.outputs({...})Requests target the producer rather than the model.
model.request_contact_attributes(...)solver.outputs({...}, contacts=contacts)Contact-indexed outputs are bound explicitly to their storage.
solver.update_contacts(...)solver.step(..., outputs=outputs)Outputs are produced with the step, avoiding a separate update protocol.

Before

Model-driven allocation
model.request_state_attributes("body_parent_f")
model.request_contact_attributes("force")

state = model.state()
contacts = model.contacts()

solver.step(state_in, state_out, control, contacts, dt)
solver.update_contacts(contacts, state_out)

parent_wrench = state_out.body_parent_f
contact_force = contacts.force

After

Solver-driven allocation
outputs = solver.outputs(
    {
        SolverOutputFlags.BODY_PARENT_F,
        SolverOutputFlags.CONTACT_F,
    },
    contacts=contacts,
)

solver.step(state_in, state_out, control, contacts, dt, outputs=outputs)

parent_wrench = outputs.body_parent_f
contact_force = outputs.contact_f

Benefits and future-proofing

This is more than moving arrays. It establishes a stable extension point between solvers and optional consumers while keeping model and state APIs focused on simulation data.

01

Clear ownership

Users ask the solver for solver outputs. The API location matches the component with the capability and implementation.

02

Pay only for what is used

Optional arrays are absent until requested, reducing memory and avoiding unnecessary diagnostic computation.

03

Independent extension

Custom solvers add flags and fields without editing Newton's global state schema or coordinating enum bit assignments.

04

Composable consumers

Sensors, viewers, loggers, and applications publish requirements as sets that can be unioned into one allocation.

05

Stronger validation

Unsupported flags, wrong concrete types, solver mismatches, and contact-buffer mismatches fail close to allocation or step.

06

Room to evolve

Future output families—iterations, residuals, thermal fields, stresses, actuator diagnostics—can follow the same contract.

Scope boundary: this migration covers built-in solver-produced diagnostics. Custom model, state, control, and contact attributes remain valid for authored or persistent simulation data.
